items.title: America is still beating China in the AI race
items.author: Noah Smith
items.blurb: Smith argues the US is staying ahead of China in the AI race, though the costs of maintaining that lead are still unknown.

items.title: Anthropic AI ‘formalizes’ proof of Fermat’s last theorem in just 11 days
items.author: Davide Castelvecchi
items.blurb: Claude produced a 13-million-line, computer-checked proof of Fermat’s last theorem in 11 days, and mathematicians now expect AI to scrutinize, and perhaps overturn, results across the whole library of mathematics.

items.title: Has the A.I. Job Apocalypse Been Postponed?
items.author: John Cassidy
items.blurb: The spread of models like Claude and ChatGPT has not yet produced mass displacement of workers, but deployment is accelerating and economic pressures are rising.

items.title: AI keeps stubbornly refusing to take our jobs
items.author: Noah Smith
items.blurb: A Labor Day look at why, despite rapid AI adoption, human labor is still valuable and the predicted job losses keep failing to show up in the data.

items.title: AI Has Solved One of Math’s $1 Million Millennium Prize Problems
items.author: Konstantin Kakaes
items.blurb: OpenAI agents proved the Navier-Stokes equations can blow up in three dimensions, with the proof verified in Lean — but Kakaes reports a competing NYU group, and both teams built on techniques from mathematicians Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa.

items.title: OpenAI claims huge maths breakthrough on a famed ‘Millennium Problem’
items.author: Davide Castelvecchi
items.blurb: Castelvecchi reports OpenAI’s claim to have cracked the physics of fluids using AI, solving one of the toughest puzzles in mathematics and a famed Millennium Problem.

items.title: The World Bank is right to prioritize reproducibility
items.blurb: A Nature editorial applauds the World Bank for publishing and verifying the raw data and code behind its research-based reports and papers, and says other agencies should follow.

items.title: No Doing, No Learning
items.author: Alex Tabarrok
items.blurb: Tabarrok argues that when regulation prevents an industry — nuclear power, engineered microbes — from ever existing, the loss is invisible: no one learns what they never got to do.

items.title: OpenAI's apparent maths breakthrough raises profound questions
items.blurb: The Economist says OpenAI’s claimed Navier-Stokes result has stirred controversy not just over who got there first but over how mathematics as a discipline should work once machines do the proving.

items.title: The Einstein test: what happens when AI tries to rediscover relativity?
items.author: Philip Ball
items.blurb: Philip Ball reports on scientists probing whether language models trained only on historical data can reproduce creative breakthroughs like relativity, a test of whether AI can genuinely discover rather than recall.

items.title: Popular open-science platform to stop hosting data and code amid funding concerns
items.author: Dalmeet Singh Chawla
items.blurb: The Open Science Framework will stop hosting data and code from November amid funding concerns, Chawla reports, forcing researchers to reconsider where their reproducibility materials live.

items.title: I Worked on Safety at OpenAI. The Fix Isn’t Hard.
items.author: Steven Adler

items.title: The Sadness of Being the ‘Last Man’
items.author: Gal Beckerman

items.title: Mothers for Sale
items.author: Helen Lewis

items.title: Trump’s Census Overhaul Would Exclude Some Immigrants and Remove Questions on Race
items.author: Zolan Kanno-Youngs

items.title: China warns bankers not to flood IPO market
Justice Dept. Investigates Nvidia Deal With Groq
items.author: Lauren Hirsch and David McCabe

items.title: The Mathematician Crushed Between OpenAI and Anthropic Over a Math Problem
items.author: Kenneth Chang
items.blurb: Kenneth Chang profiles Tristan Buckmaster, who was closing in on a Navier–Stokes proof when an AI lab's resources got there first — a case study in what AI does to human research careers.

items.title: Mathematicians confront the AI apocalypse
items.blurb: Scientific American asks what happens to mathematics as a discipline once machines outpace its brightest practitioners.

items.title: Economic Scenarios for Transformative AI
items.author: Tyler Cowen
items.blurb: Cowen flags a new Korinek–Jones et al. framework from Anthropic for assessing the economic effects of transformative AI, praising it as sober and dynamically consistent.

items.title: AI researchers reckon with the $1.5 million ‘academia tax’
items.author: Ben Deighton
items.blurb: Nature's Ben Deighton on why AI researchers forgo seven-figure industry pay for academic freedom, and the hybrid models that may let them have both.

items.title: A Natural Solution to the Replication Crisis in Science
items.author: Orit Peleg
items.blurb: Orit Peleg argues in Nautilus that scientists should borrow from ant colonies' distributed, redundant verification to fix reproducibility.

items.title: Deep theorems were scarce and difficult and so became an effective mechanism to identify deep thought. AI has broken this system.
items.author: Bryna Kra
items.blurb: In a guest post on Terence Tao’s blog, Bryna Kra argues that AI has broken the system in which proving hard theorems served as mathematics’ signal of deep thought, and calls for incentives that reward exposition and understanding rather than theorem counts.

items.title: After Math
items.author: Silvia De Toffoli and Eamon Duede
items.blurb: Philosophers De Toffoli and Duede argue that OpenAI’s Navier–Stokes result is an answer rather than a solution: a formally certified but opaque proof does not deliver the intelligibility that mathematics exists to produce.

items.title: Wimbledon, the U.S. Open, and the future of mathematics
items.author: Steven Strogatz
items.blurb: Strogatz uses Wimbledon and the U.S. Open as two visions of mathematics’ future — one prizing style and understanding, the other brash and democratic — and admits ambivalence about what AI proof-generation might cost the discipline.

items.title: Happy, those able to know the causes of things
items.author: Nestor Guillen
items.blurb: Guillen argues that large language models are cultural technologies synthesising humanity’s accumulated mathematics, so their discoveries should be a source of communal pride — and are probably confined to the ‘convex hull’ of existing ideas.

items.title: A simple model of AI-aided economic growth
items.author: Tyler Cowen
items.blurb: Cowen sketches a two-factor growth model in which AI floods the economy with ‘intelligence’ while Polanyi-style tacit knowledge stays scarce, predicting rising returns, employment and real wages in the sector that holds it.

items.title: The mathematicians rebel against AI
items.author: Tyler Cowen
items.blurb: Cowen reads the Fields Medallists’ declaration sympathetically but disputes its claim that the outcome hinges on the humans running the labs, arguing the real action variable is how well mathematicians adapt and what work they choose to reward.

items.title: Diversity Is Our Strength?
items.author: Alex Tabarrok
items.blurb: Tabarrok flags a pre-registered scoping review of more than 100 papers finding that only 15–28 percent of reported results support the claim that diversity improves scientific output or impact.

items.title: Labor reallocation during the Industrial Revolution
items.author: Tyler Cowen
items.blurb: Cowen highlights Hillary Vipond’s study of 170 million British census records: when bootmaking mechanised, 153,000 artisanal jobs vanished and 140,000 new ones appeared, but the adjustment fell on young entrants rather than displaced incumbents.
